title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
hook: a man gets a ghost who will do any job, but will kill him the moment it runs out of work

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: a banyan seed, broken open. Too fine to see, too real to deny. Today, the karma road, with Vivekananda's lectures and a ghost story.
screen: `TOO FINE TO SEE, TOO REAL TO DENY.`

segments.voice: A man wants a ghost to do his bidding. A sage gives him a charm, and the ghost appears: I'll do anything you command. But the moment I have nothing to do, I'll kill you. The man thinks: perfect. Build me a palace. Done. Bring me money. Done. Clear this forest. Done. Every job, finished in minutes. And with rising panic, the man realizes he's running out of jobs. It sounds like a folk tale. Swami Vivekananda told it lecturing on karma yoga in the 1890s.
screen: `A GHOST THAT DOES ANY JOB.` → `EVERY JOB, DONE IN MINUTES.` → `RUNNING OUT OF WORK.`

segments.voice: The man runs back to the sage. The sage says: see that dog with the curly tail? Tell the ghost to straighten it. The ghost pulls the tail straight. Lets go. It curls right back. Straightens it. Lets go. Curls. The ghost is at it day after day, the story says, until it gives up and makes peace with the man. Then Vivekananda explains. The world is like that dog's curly tail. People have been trying to straighten it for a very long time; every generation thinks it will finally fix things for good, and the tail curls back. So why work to help anyone at all? His surprising answer is the title of that lecture: we help ourselves, not the world. The world doesn't need us to save it. It will go on, with its ups and downs. But the one who serves is changed by serving. Vivekananda called the world a great moral gymnasium, a place where we build strength by working in it. So he turns charity upside down. When you help someone, don't feel proud. Be grateful. They gave you the chance to practice. That's why karma yoga can work without discouragement. You're not failing if the tail curls back; you were never really in charge of the tail. You're in charge of the work, and of the heart you bring to it. This isn't giving up on the world. Vivekananda himself founded a mission that still runs hospitals, schools and disaster relief. It's working without needing to win.
screen: `STRAIGHTEN THE DOG'S TAIL.` · `IT CURLS RIGHT BACK.` · `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.` · `BE GRATEFUL TO THE ONE YOU HELP.` · then, large: `WORK WITHOUT NEEDING TO WIN.`

segments.voice: Think of one problem that keeps curling back, a mess that returns, a conflict that won't settle, a cause that never seems to move, and let yourself feel the tiredness of it. Breathe in and let go of needing it fixed forever; breathe out and hold on to the next small, good action, then quietly thank one person you've helped for the chance. If you pray, you can offer that thanks.
Karma. Action. In Vivekananda's lecture, good work doesn't straighten the world's tail. It straightens the worker.
Your line: the world's curly tail. Straightening it was never the point. Day three hundred eleven, done.

howItsDone: The Ramakrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda, runs schools, hospitals and disaster relief as spiritual practice, and its monks and volunteers are taught to see service as a privilege rather than charity.
